q: How does a difference matte isolate a subject?
options: It compares the footage against a clean plate of the empty set and keeps what changed
It samples the green screen color and turns matching pixels transparent
It uses the overall brightness of a second matte layer to cut out the transparency
It uses a hand-animated rotoscoped shape drawn around the moving subject on each frame
why: A difference matte subtracts a clean plate (the same shot without the subject) from the footage — whatever differs between the two is the subject.
options_original: It compares the footage against a clean plate of the empty set and keeps what changed
It samples the solid green screen color and turns every matching pixel transparent
It uses the overall brightness of a second matte layer to cut out the transparency
It draws a hand-animated rotoscoped shape around the moving subject on every frame

q: Why are green and blue the standard colors for keying screens?
options: They happen to be the cheapest paint colors to manufacture in bulk
Camera sensors simply cannot record any green or blue light
They make the recorded footage compress down into much smaller files
They are far from human skin tones, so subjects separate cleanly
why: Keying works by removing a color; choosing one distant from skin tones means the keyer can pull the screen without eating into the actor.

q: What does a point tracker actually follow in the footage?
options: The loudest audio peaks in the film's soundtrack
The selected layer's built-in alpha channel
A distinct pattern of pixels from frame to frame
The hidden metadata embedded by the camera
why: A point tracker locks onto a recognizable pixel pattern and follows it frame by frame, producing position data you can apply to other layers.

q: Why do studios often render finished shots to OpenEXR sequences even though the files are large?
options: EXR stores high-dynamic-range color and extra channels needed for post-production
EXR files stream smoothly to websites and mobile phones without conversion
EXR embeds the project's finished audio mix inside each frame of the sequence
EXR is the image format that modern real-time game engines require for import
why: EXR holds far more color precision than standard formats plus extra data channels (like depth), giving compositors room to adjust shots without quality loss.
options_original: EXR stores high-dynamic-range color and extra channels needed for post-production
EXR files stream smoothly across any website or mobile phone without needing conversion
EXR automatically embeds the project's finished audio mix inside every frame of the sequence
EXR is the only image format that modern real-time game engines are able to import at all

q: What is Apple ProRes mainly used for?
options: High-quality masters and handing footage between post-production teams
Streaming compressed video over social media using very minimal bandwidth
Compressing spoken-word audio files for podcasts and radio broadcasts
Storing detailed 3D character models for real-time game engines
why: ProRes is an intermediate codec: large files, high quality, and smooth editing performance — ideal for masters and post handoffs, not for web streaming.

q: Compared with H.264, what is the main drawback of H.265 (HEVC)?
options: It produces noticeably larger files at the same quality level
It is not as universally supported across devices and platforms
It cannot store full-color video footage
It requires rendered image sequences instead of a video file
why: H.265 compresses more efficiently than H.264, but playback support is less universal, which matters when the target is 'everything, everywhere.'
options_original: It produces noticeably larger files at exactly the same quality level
It is not as universally supported across devices and platforms
It is completely unable to store any full-color video footage at all
It only works when placed inside rendered image sequences on disk

q: Which device is best described as a mixed reality headset that lets holograms interact with real surfaces?
options: Microsoft HoloLens 2
HTC Vive
A standard desktop monitor
A green-screen stage
why: HoloLens 2 maps the real environment and anchors holograms to it, so digital objects can sit on real tables and walls; the Vive is a VR headset that replaces your view.

q: A film-quality 3D character is being converted for a standalone VR headset. What is typically required?
options: Increasing the polygon count, adding more textures, and boosting the lighting for detail
Removing textures, deleting materials, and stripping the lights from the model
Rendering the character out as a flat 2D image sequence and mapping it onto a card
Reducing polygons, simplifying materials, and baking lighting to fit the performance budget
why: Standalone headsets have limited processing power, so film assets must be optimized — fewer polygons, simpler shaders, baked lighting — to hold the required frame rate.
options_original: Increasing the polygon count, adding more textures, and boosting all the lighting for detail
Removing all textures, deleting the materials, and stripping every light from the model
Rendering the character out as a flat 2D image sequence and mapping it onto a card
Reducing polygons, simplifying materials, and baking lighting to fit the performance budget

q: Which practice best protects a client deliverable sent over the internet?
options: Posting the private download link openly in a public forum for everyone's convenience
Emailing the account password inside the very same message that contains the link
Restricting access to specific accounts and using passwords or expiring links
Uploading the deliverable to a fully public repository so the client can find it easily
why: Limiting access to named accounts, adding a password sent through a separate channel, and expiring the link all shrink the window for a leak.

q: When should quality assurance happen in an animation production?
options: Only during the final render checks before delivery
Continuously, during every phase of production
Only when the client requests a review
Only during pre-production planning
why: The standard says quality assurance is monitored concurrent with all phases — problems caught early (in boards or concepts) are far cheaper to fix than problems found after rendering.

q: What does "artisanship" mean when critiquing a texture or model?
options: How quickly and efficiently the artist managed to finish the work
How expensive the professional software used to make the work was
How famous and well known the artist who made the work happens to be
The level of technical skill and craft quality shown in the work
why: Artisanship is about craft — clean construction, believable materials, solid technique — regardless of who made it, how fast, or with what tools.

q: A storyboard is technically clean, but the scene reads as comedic when the script calls for suspense. Which critique category has the problem?
options: Tone
Artisanship
Scheduling
Distribution
why: Tone asks whether the work matches the emotional intent of the project. The craft (artisanship) is fine here — the feeling is wrong.

q: What are "dailies" at an animation studio?
options: The total number of individual frames the render farm outputs during each working day
The daily pay rate that freelance artists at the studio earn for their work
Regular review sessions where the team looks at work in progress and gives feedback
Backup copies of all the project files that get made at the very end of each day
why: Dailies are recurring review meetings where directors, leads, and artists critique in-progress shots so problems get caught early.

q: When is the best time to hold a project postmortem?
options: Shortly after the project is completed, while details are still fresh
Well before any real production work on the project has actually begun
Right in the middle of the studio's single busiest production week
Only in the rare case that the entire project completely failed
why: The standard calls for reviewing workflow after completion — and doing it soon after wrap means the team still remembers what actually happened. Successful projects deserve postmortems too.

q: A render is beautifully lit and detailed, but audiences can't tell what is happening in the shot. Which critique category is failing?
options: Artisanship
Tone
File management
Effectiveness
why: Effectiveness asks whether the piece does its job — a shot's job is to communicate. Gorgeous but confusing means the craft succeeded and the communication failed.

q: Why should concept art and storyboards be critiqued early instead of waiting until models and renders are done?
options: Because the studio's concept artists outrank the other artists
Because paying clients look mainly at the early concept art
Because problems are cheaper and faster to fix before later phases build on the work
Because tone is decided at the storyboard stage and cannot change later
why: Every later phase depends on the earlier ones. Fixing a story problem in boards takes a conversation; fixing it after animation and rendering can take weeks.
options_original: Because the studio's own concept artists will always outrank all of the other artists
Because paying clients only ever bother to look at the early concept art
Because problems are cheaper and faster to fix before later phases build on the work
Because the storyboard stage is the only phase where a project's tone matters

q: Which communication practice helps an animation team succeed?
options: Giving specific, actionable feedback during reviews
Keeping notes vague and unclear so no one gets offended
Routing every message through a single controlling person
Waiting until the final delivery to first mention any concerns
why: Specific, actionable notes give artists a clear path to fix problems. Vague or delayed feedback lets problems grow more expensive.

q: During a postmortem, what should the team focus on?
options: Determining exactly whose fault each separate mistake was
Only celebrating all of the things that went right
Rewriting and fully re-editing the already finished film
The process and workflow, not blaming individuals
why: Blame teaches people to hide problems; examining the process honestly — both wins and failures — is what actually improves the next project.

q: In a studio review, what is a "retake"?
options: Filming an entire live-action reference video all over again from scratch
A note asking an artist to revise a shot so it meets quality standards
A duplicate backup copy made of the studio's final delivered render
A scheduled rest break that the whole team takes in between shots
why: A retake is a revision note that comes out of review. It's a normal part of quality assurance — the system catching something before delivery.

q: A team keeps missing deadlines because two departments unknowingly do the same work twice. What kind of problem is this?
options: A sudden and total failure of the studio's core rendering hardware
A disagreement between the artists over the project's overall artistic style
A breakdown in organization and communication between departments
A subtle and hard-to-trace bug hidden inside the rendering software
why: Duplicated work means the departments aren't coordinating — an organizational and communication failure, which this standard asks you to recognize as a key success factor.

q: What is a good length for a student or junior artist's demo reel?
options: Short — roughly one to two minutes of only your best work
At least ten minutes, to show everything you've made
Exactly thirty seconds, no matter how much strong work you have
As long as possible, including every class project
why: Industry guidance favors short, curated reels — reviewers remember your weakest shot, so a tight reel of strong work beats a long mixed one.

q: What should go into your portfolio or demo reel?
options: Every project that you have completed
Mainly the work you made in team or group settings
Mostly online tutorials that you followed along step by step
Your strongest work, chosen to match the job you want
why: The standard calls for appropriate subject matter and quality — that means curating your best pieces and targeting them at the role you're pursuing.
options_original: Every single project that you have ever fully completed
Only the work that you happened to make in team or group settings
Mostly online tutorials that you followed along step by step
Your strongest work, chosen to match the job you want

q: What is the most common way to distribute a demo reel or portfolio today?
options: Handing out physically printed paper copies of several individual frames from it
Posting it online (personal website, Vimeo, ArtStation) and linking it in applications
Emailing the large raw project source files directly to studios
Showing the reel in person, when a studio requests a private meeting
why: Reels live online now — hosted on a site or platform and linked from applications, profiles, and email signatures so anyone can view them instantly.
options_original: Handing out physically printed paper copies of several individual frames from it
Posting it online (personal website, Vimeo, ArtStation) and linking it in applications
Emailing the huge raw project source files directly to every single studio
Showing the reel only in person, and solely when a studio first requests a private meeting

q: Why should you research a company before applying to it?
options: So you can tailor your reel, résumé, and cover letter to that studio's style and needs
So you can copy their animation style into your student work
Because hiring studios require applicants to pass a company history quiz
So you can list all of their main industry competitors right in your cover letter
why: Knowing what a studio makes and which roles it hires lets you present the most relevant version of yourself — generic applications usually go nowhere.
options_original: So you can tailor your reel, résumé, and cover letter to that studio's style and needs
So you can copy their exact animation style straight into your student work overnight
Because most hiring studios require every applicant to pass a company history quiz first
So you can list all of their main industry competitors right in your cover letter

q: What belongs on an animation résumé?
options: Long, rambling paragraphs that tell the reader your full personal life story
Relevant skills, software, education, and experience presented clearly
Your grade point average and little else
Large full-page screenshots from each of your projects
why: A résumé is a clear, scannable summary of your relevant qualifications — the reel shows the art; the résumé shows the facts.
options_original: Long, rambling paragraphs that tell the reader your full personal life story
Relevant skills, software, education, and experience presented clearly
Only your final grade point average and nothing else at all besides that
Large full-page screenshots taken from every single one of your projects

q: In an interview, how should you handle questions about your demo reel?
options: Be ready to explain what you did on each shot and how you did it
Take full personal credit for the whole team's work to look much stronger
Simply say that the reel speaks for itself and politely decline to elaborate
Carefully avoid all of the technical details so that you seem modest
why: Interviewers want your process and your honest role in each shot — being able to walk through your work shot by shot proves the reel really is yours.

q: What is an animatic?
options: The final, fully rendered, color-graded and delivered version of an animated film
A written master list of a project's main characters and locations
Storyboard panels edited together with timing and often temporary sound to preview the story
A downloadable software plug-in that automatically animates the characters for you
why: An animatic is a moving storyboard — panels cut together with timing and temp audio so the story can be felt and judged before final animation is made.
options_original: The completely final, fully rendered, color-graded and delivered version of an animated film
A written master list of every one of a project's many main characters and its locations
Storyboard panels edited together with timing and often temporary sound to preview the story
A downloadable software plug-in that automatically animates the characters for you

q: Which approach makes a pitch most effective?
options: Covering each small plot detail so nothing is left out
A clear, concise idea supported by strong visuals
Reading the entire script aloud to the room
Using no visuals so people focus on your words
why: Pitches succeed on clarity and impact — a focused idea plus compelling visuals (like an animatic) respects the audience's time and leaves them wanting more.
options_original: Covering every small plot detail so that nothing is left out
A clear, concise idea supported by strong visuals
Reading the entire script aloud to the room
Using no visuals so people focus only on your words

q: Besides job hunting, what is another professional use for a strong reel or portfolio?
options: Replacing the need for written client contracts
Avoiding the fees involved in registering a new business
Attracting clients or investors to fund a project or studio
Guaranteeing that you will win a major film festival award
why: The standard names work, employment, and investment — the same reel that convinces an employer can convince a client or investor that a project is worth funding.
options_original: Completely replacing the need for any written client contracts at all
Avoiding all of the fees involved when first registering a new business
Attracting clients or investors to fund a project or studio
Guaranteeing that you will win a major film festival award

q: Why should you include a shot breakdown with your demo reel?
options: It tells reviewers exactly what work you personally did on each shot
It makes the final exported video file much smaller and faster to upload
It replaces the need to submit a separate written résumé
It proves that you own valid licenses for the software used
why: Especially on team projects, a breakdown honestly credits your contribution — and honesty matters, because studios verify claims and talk to each other.
options_original: It tells reviewers exactly what work you personally did on each shot
It makes the final exported video file much smaller and faster to upload
It completely replaces the need to also submit a separate written résumé
It clearly proves that you own valid licenses for all of the software used

q: Which program is built mainly for compositing and motion graphics rather than 3D modeling?
options: Adobe After Effects
ZBrush
Autodesk Maya
Substance 3D Painter
why: After Effects is a compositing and motion-graphics tool; ZBrush sculpts, Maya models and animates in 3D, and Substance Painter textures 3D models.

q: A digital painter wants brush strokes that get thicker as she presses harder. Which hardware provides that?
options: A larger monitor
A pressure-sensitive drawing tablet
More system memory (RAM)
A faster solid-state drive
why: A pressure-sensitive pen tablet reports how hard the pen is pressed, so painting software can vary stroke size and opacity like a real brush.

q: A large 3D scene crashes while loading because the computer runs out of working memory. Which upgrade addresses this most directly?
options: A higher-resolution webcam
A second keyboard
More system memory (RAM)
A larger desk speaker
why: RAM is the computer's working memory; scenes with many high-resolution textures and objects need more of it to load and stay open.

q: Which keyboard shortcut undoes the last action in most creative programs?
options: Ctrl+V (Cmd+V on Mac)
Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on Mac)
Ctrl+P (Cmd+P on Mac)
Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac)
why: Ctrl+Z / Cmd+Z is the near-universal undo shortcut; Ctrl+V pastes, Ctrl+S saves, and Ctrl+P prints.

q: A program freezes on a Windows computer. Which built-in tool lets you see the frozen program and end it?
options: Task Manager
The display settings panel
The desktop wallpaper menu
The printer queue
why: Task Manager lists running programs and their resource use and lets you end a task that has stopped responding (Activity Monitor or Force Quit does this on a Mac).

q: Why should project file names avoid spaces and special characters such as # or &?
options: Spaces and symbols add extra data that makes every file noticeably larger on disk
Some programs, servers, and web addresses misread them, which can break links and scripts
Those characters quietly convert the file into a different format when it is saved
Symbols in a name erase the file's earlier saved versions from the version history
why: Spaces and symbols can be interpreted as commands or separators by software, servers, and URLs, so studios stick to letters, numbers, underscores, and hyphens.

q: Two artists open and save the same scene file at once, and one overwrites the other's work. Which practice prevents this?
options: Saving the scene under shorter file names so each save finishes faster
Compressing the scene into a zip file before each person opens it
Checking the file out (locking it) so one person edits at a time
Turning off autosave so the program never writes over the file by itself
why: Check-out or file locking in an asset-management system lets one person edit a file at a time, so changes are not lost to overwrites.

q: A program starts crashing right after an operating-system update. What is a sensible first troubleshooting step?
options: Reformat the hard drive and reinstall the operating system from scratch
Replace the computer, since the update has damaged the hardware
Delete the project folder so the program starts with a clean slate
Check for and install an updated version of the program or its drivers
why: Updates can break compatibility; installing the program's latest version or updated graphics drivers is the first, least destructive fix to try.

q: Renders are failing because the startup drive is nearly full. What is the best fix?
options: Free up space by archiving old projects to another drive
Lower the monitor brightness so the computer uses less power while rendering
Unplug the mouse and keyboard so the render gets more system resources
Raise the screen resolution so the render engine has more room to work
why: Renders and caches need free disk space; moving finished projects to archive storage frees room without losing work.

q: Ransomware encrypts a studio's files and demands payment. Which preparation best lets the studio recover without paying?
options: A faster internet connection for downloading files
Recent backups kept offline or offsite
Larger monitors so damage is easier to spot
Renaming the project folders each week
why: Backups stored offline or offsite cannot be encrypted by the attack, so the studio can wipe the infected systems and restore its files.

q: Which password practice best protects a studio account?
options: Reusing one strong password on many sites
Writing the password on a sticky note on the monitor
A long, unique passphrase plus two-factor authentication
Emailing the password to the whole team
why: A long unique passphrase resists guessing, and two-factor authentication blocks access even if the password leaks; reuse and sharing spread the risk.

q: Which technology records an actor's facial expressions so they can drive a digital character's face?
options: Rotoscoping
Camera tracking
Photogrammetry
Facial (performance) capture
why: Facial capture tracks the actor's face, often with head-mounted cameras, and transfers the expressions to the character's facial rig.

q: A team photographs a real statue from dozens of angles so software can build a textured 3D model of it. What is this called?
options: Photogrammetry
Motion capture
Keyframing
UV unwrapping
why: Photogrammetry reconstructs 3D shape and texture from many overlapping photographs of a real object.

q: An illustrator wants to keep every layer editable for later changes. Which file format should she save her Photoshop work in?
options: JPEG
PSD
GIF
PNG
why: PSD is Photoshop's native working format and keeps layers, masks, and adjustments editable; JPEG, GIF, and PNG save a flattened image.

q: Which storage choice best suits a team whose shared project files must stay in sync?
options: Each artist keeps their own copy on a personal USB stick
Artists email the latest files to each other after every change
A central network server or managed cloud storage
Everyone saves copies on their own desktop and compares them weekly
why: A central server or managed cloud drive gives everyone one current copy of each file, with permissions and backups in one place.

q: Halfway through production, a client asks for a new character that is not in the design brief. What is the professional response?
options: Add the character quietly and hope the existing schedule still holds
Ignore the request, since it was not written into the original brief
Stop replying to the client until they agree to drop the new request
Treat it as a scope change and agree on schedule and budget first
why: New work outside the brief is a scope change; professionals confirm how it affects time and cost before committing to it.

q: Which item usually belongs in a design brief?
options: The target audience and delivery platform
The home addresses and phone numbers of every artist on the team
A list of the keyboard shortcuts each artist prefers to use
The studio's lunch schedule and office cleaning rotation
why: A brief defines who the work is for and where it will be shown, which drives style, technical limits, and priorities.

q: A project will be shown on a large cinema screen. How does that change texture planning compared with a mobile game?
options: Textures should be kept smaller than on mobile so the film loads quickly
Higher-resolution textures are affordable and needed for close-up detail
Cinema projects skip textures and rely on lighting alone for surface detail
Textures have to be black and white because projectors handle color separately
why: Film renders are not limited by a phone's memory and are seen huge on screen, so detailed high-resolution textures are expected.

q: Why do studios build reusable libraries of props, furniture, and materials?
options: Libraries force every scene in the film to look identical to the others
Reused assets are locked, so they cannot be changed for a new shot
Reusing proven assets saves time and keeps quality consistent across shots
An asset library replaces the need for a design brief on each project
why: Building an asset once and reusing it with variations saves production time and keeps a consistent look and quality level.

q: In the file name SC02_SH040_anim_v007.ma, what does v007 tell the team?
options: It is the scene number within the film
It is the shot number within the scene
It is the number of seconds the shot lasts
It is the seventh saved version of that file
why: The v-number is the version; SC02 is the scene, SH040 the shot, and anim the department.

q: Why name 3D objects (for example L_arm_ctrl) instead of leaving default names like pCube27?
options: Clear names let anyone find and script the right objects
Objects with names render faster than objects with default names
Scenes containing default object names cannot be saved to disk
Naming an object changes its display color so it is easier to see
why: Consistent descriptive names make large scenes navigable for the whole team and let scripts and rigs find objects reliably.

q: Which of these is a principle of design rather than an element of design?
options: Line
Balance
Shape
Color
why: Elements are the building blocks (line, shape, color, value, texture); principles such as balance, emphasis, and rhythm describe how they are arranged.

q: An artist places a bright red character against a gray, muted background. Which design principle is she using to guide the viewer's eye?
options: Rhythm through repetition
Symmetrical balance
Emphasis through contrast
Proportion
why: Strong color contrast creates a focal point, which is the principle of emphasis.

q: Why do artists block in a figure with simple shapes such as spheres, cylinders, and boxes before adding detail?
options: Printers require artwork to be built from simple geometric shapes
The shapes hide drawing mistakes so they do not show in the final art
Using basic shapes removes the need to look at any reference material
It sets proportion, volume, and perspective before detail
why: Constructing with basic forms establishes the figure's structure in 3D space first; detail added on top then stays in proportion.

q: What is a thumbnail sketch?
options: A small, quick drawing used to explore ideas and compositions
A finished, fully colored illustration ready to show the client
A rough 3D blockout model used to test a scene's layout
A low-resolution texture used on small props far from the camera
why: Thumbnails are tiny, fast sketches that let an artist try many ideas before committing to one.

q: Why do animators study reference footage of real people and animals?
options: To copy the footage frame by frame into the final film
To observe how weight, timing, and anatomy really move
To avoid drawing hands and feet
To replace the storyboard
why: Reference shows how real bodies shift weight and time their motions, which animators then interpret and exaggerate.

q: What is a character turnaround (model sheet)?
options: A list of the lines of dialogue the character speaks
A final 3D render of the character placed in its finished shot
Drawings of the character from several angles for consistency
A chart of the color palette used across the film's scenes
why: A turnaround shows the character from front, side, back, and three-quarter views so modelers and artists keep the design on-model.

q: Why do designers give a main character a limited, consistent color palette?
options: A small palette lowers the time needed to render the character
Animation studios are legally required to limit each character's colors
A limited palette removes the need to light the character in each scene
It makes the character instantly recognizable and readable on screen
why: A small, consistent set of colors helps a character read clearly and stay recognizable across shots and merchandise.

q: A heavy object starts moving slowly, speeds up, and then slows down before it stops. Which principle is this?
options: Slow in and slow out
Squash and stretch
Staging
Exaggeration
why: Slow in and slow out (easing) places more frames near the start and end of a move, so motion accelerates and decelerates naturally.

q: A character's pose and the camera framing are set up so the audience understands the action and mood at a glance. Which principle is this?
options: Secondary action
Staging
Solid drawing
Follow through
why: Staging presents an idea so it is unmistakably clear, using pose, composition, and camera placement.

q: While a character walks, she also whistles and glances at her phone. Which principle do the whistling and glancing represent?
options: Anticipation
Arcs
Secondary action
Timing
why: Secondary actions are smaller actions that support the main action (walking) and add personality without stealing focus.

q: In a storyboard panel, what does an arrow drawn over the image usually show?
options: The panel has been rejected and should be removed from the board
The direction the scene's main light is coming from
The location where the next scene in the film takes place
Movement of a character or the camera within the shot
why: Storyboard arrows indicate direction of movement, either a character's action or a camera move such as a pan or push-in.

q: In a typical 3D pipeline, which step has to happen before a character can be animated?
options: Rigging
Compositing
Final rendering
Color grading
why: Animators pose characters through a rig, so rigging (building the skeleton and controls) comes before animation.

q: Why does texturing usually come after modeling in the pipeline?
options: Applying textures first makes the modeling stage go much faster
Textures map onto the surface, so the shape and UVs come first
Textures are applied during compositing, after the render is finished
Modeling tools delete any textures that were applied before them
why: Textures are laid onto a model's UVs; if the shape changed afterward, the textures would stretch or need redoing.

q: A modeler starts with a low-poly cage and applies a modifier that produces a smooth, rounded surface. Which technique is this?
options: Boolean subtraction
Photogrammetry
Subdivision surface modeling
Particle simulation
why: Subdivision repeatedly splits and smooths the faces of a simple cage, giving a smooth surface that stays easy to edit.

q: Which tool pulls selected faces outward to create new geometry, such as a branch growing from a tree trunk?
options: Delete
Merge
Smooth shading
Extrude
why: Extrude pushes faces or edges out and builds new connecting geometry, a core polygon-modeling operation.

q: Digital sculpting is most like working with which traditional material?
options: Clay
Watercolor
Stained glass
Woodblock printing
why: Sculpting programs push, pull, and smooth a dense mesh much like shaping clay by hand.

q: Which subject is best described as organic?
options: A metal robot arm
A tree trunk
A car door
A steel bolt
why: Organic forms are flowing, natural shapes such as plants, creatures, and bodies; machined objects are hard-surface.

q: When a hard-surface model is smoothed, its edges turn soft and rounded. Which technique keeps edges crisp?
options: Flipping the normals on the faces along each edge
Lowering the texture resolution so the edges look sharper
Adding support edge loops or bevels near the edges
Deleting the UVs so the smoothing has nothing to follow
why: Extra edge loops placed close to an edge (or a bevel) hold the shape tight when subdivision smooths the model.

q: What is UV unwrapping?
options: Adding and positioning lights around a model before rendering
Animating a camera so it moves around the model in a full circle
Deleting the faces of a model that the camera cannot see
Flattening a 3D surface into 2D so a texture can be applied
why: UV unwrapping lays a model's surface flat, like a cut-open box, so a 2D image can map back onto it accurately.

q: Which projection is the natural first choice for texturing a basketball?
options: Spherical mapping
Planar mapping
Cylindrical mapping
No mapping
why: Spherical mapping wraps an image around a ball shape like a globe, matching a basketball's form.

q: In a UV layout, two UV shells sit directly on top of each other. What problem will that cause?
options: The model becomes invisible in the viewport and in renders
The same texture pixels appear on both areas of the model
The model's polygon count doubles when the scene is saved
The model's animation stops playing until the shells are moved
why: Overlapping shells share the same texture space, so painting one area also paints the other unless that mirroring is intended.

q: Before texturing, a modeler finds duplicate vertices stacked in the same spot. What should she do?
options: Leave them in place so the model has more detail to work with
Color them red so the texture artist knows to paint around them
Merge them so the mesh is clean and properly connected
Add more vertices on top of them to make the area stronger
why: Duplicate vertices cause shading seams and broken edges; merging them produces a clean, connected mesh.

q: Which rendering method calculates reflections and shadows by following the paths of light rays?
options: Phong shading
Flat shading
Wireframe display
Ray tracing
why: Ray tracing simulates light rays bouncing through the scene, producing accurate reflections, refractions, and shadows.

q: In a PBR material, what does raising the roughness value do?
options: It spreads reflections so the surface looks more matte
It makes the surface look more metallic, like polished steel
It makes the surface more transparent, like frosted glass
It makes the surface emit its own light, like a neon sign
why: Roughness controls how blurred reflections are: low roughness is mirror-like, high roughness is matte.

q: What does a normal map do?
options: It permanently raises the model's polygon count to add detail
It fakes small bumps and grooves without adding polygons
It sets the color and brightness of the lights in the scene
It controls where the render camera focuses and how much blur appears
why: A normal map stores surface directions in an image, so lighting shows fine detail on a low-poly model.

q: Which dynamics tool would you use to make a stack of wooden crates topple and collide?
options: Cloth simulation
Hair grooming
Rigid-body simulation
UV mapping
why: Rigid-body simulation handles solid objects that fall, collide, and bounce without bending.

q: Why do artists cache (bake) a finished simulation to disk?
options: To delete the simulation once it looks correct in the viewport
To change the colors of the simulated objects for the final render
To shrink the model's textures so the simulation runs faster
So it plays back and renders identically without recalculating
why: A cache stores each frame's simulation result, so playback is fast and every render matches the approved result.

q: Which light type shines a cone of light in one direction, like a flashlight?
options: Spot light
Directional light
Point light
Ambient light
why: A spot light emits a cone from one position in one direction, with adjustable cone angle and edge softness.

q: Which light type emits light from a rectangular surface and produces soft shadows, like a photographer's softbox?
options: Point light
Area light
Spot light
Directional light
why: An area light has a physical size; larger sources create softer shadow edges, similar to a softbox.

q: In three-point lighting, what is the fill light's job?
options: Separate the subject from the background
Act as the brightest main light
Soften the shadows created by the key light
Light only the background
why: The fill sits opposite the key at lower intensity and lifts the shadows; the back light separates the subject.

q: A director wants a kitchen scene to feel warm and cozy. Which lighting choice fits best?
options: Harsh, cold blue light with deep, hard-edged shadows
Flickering green light that changes intensity from frame to frame
Flat gray light from all around the set with no visible shadows
Soft, warm orange-yellow light with gentle shadows
why: Warm color temperatures and soft shadows read as comfortable and inviting.

q: A game level has fixed buildings lit by a sun that never moves. Why is baked lighting a good fit?
options: The lighting does not change, so precalculated lightmaps stay correct
Baked lighting updates instantly whenever the lights in the level move
Baking the lighting removes the need for any textures on the buildings
Baking the lighting makes the buildings animate without keyframes
why: Baked lighting is calculated once and stored; it suits static scenes because nothing changes that would make it wrong.

q: In 3D animation software, what is a keyframe?
options: A frame that has been cut out of the final film during the edit
A frame where the animator sets a pose and software fills the gaps
The first frame of each scene, which the software creates for you
A frame reserved for lining up the soundtrack with the picture
why: Animators set keys at important moments; the software interpolates the in-between frames.

q: In the graph editor, what does a flat, horizontal section of a curve mean?
options: The object is moving at its fastest speed during that part
The keyframes on that section of the curve were deleted
The value is not changing, so the object holds still on that channel
The scene is rendering, so the curve is temporarily locked in place
why: A curve shows a value over time; a flat line means no change in that value during that time.

q: At 24 frames per second, how many frames make up a 3-second shot?
why: 24 frames per second times 3 seconds equals 72 frames.

q: Which constraint makes a character's head turn automatically to face a moving target?
options: An aim (look-at) constraint
A scale constraint
A Boolean modifier
A subdivision modifier
why: An aim constraint points one axis of an object at a target, so the head follows the target as it moves.

q: A character picks up a cup and carries it. Which setup lets the cup move with her hand?
options: Baking the cup's lighting so it stays bright in her hand
A parent constraint linking the cup to the hand
Deleting the cup's keyframes so it is free to move anywhere
UV unwrapping the cup so it follows the hand's texture
why: A parent constraint makes the cup follow the hand's position and rotation while it is held.

q: What is a rig?
options: A path that the render camera follows through the scene
An arrangement of lights placed around a character model
A skeleton of joints and controls used to pose a model
A texture map that stores the color of a model's surface
why: A rig combines joints, skinning, and control objects so animators can pose and animate a character.

q: Why do riggers give animators on-screen control curves instead of having them grab joints directly?
options: Control curves make the character model render noticeably faster
Joints in a skeleton cannot be keyframed directly by animators
Control curves change the model's color so poses are easier to see
Controls are easier to select and keep the rig stable and consistent
why: Control curves are clear handles that drive the joints safely, so animators do not break the skeleton by accident.

q: Which camera move rotates the camera left or right from a fixed position?
options: Pan
Tilt
Dolly
Crane
why: A pan rotates horizontally on a fixed base; a tilt rotates up and down; dolly and crane moves change the camera's position.

q: A camera physically travels toward the subject on a track. What is this move called?
options: A zoom in
A dolly in
A pan
A tilt
why: A dolly moves the camera itself; a zoom changes focal length without moving the camera, so perspective behaves differently.

q: What does a high-angle shot looking down at a character usually suggest?
options: The character is powerful and imposing
The scene is a flashback
The character seems small or vulnerable
The camera is broken
why: Looking down on a character diminishes them visually, which often signals weakness or vulnerability.

q: An exported model appears far too large in the game engine. What should the artist check?
options: The texture resolution
The audio sample rate
The frame rate
The export scale and unit settings
why: Programs use different units (centimeters, meters); mismatched export scale makes models import at the wrong size.

q: A looping walk cycle shows a visible hitch each time it repeats in the engine. What needs fixing?
options: The end of the cycle doesn't flow seamlessly back into the start
The character model uses too many texture maps for the engine
The camera angle in the engine is set too low for the walk
The footstep audio in the engine is set too quiet to hear
why: For a clean loop, the last frames must flow back into the first; a mismatched or duplicated end pose causes a pop each time it repeats.

q: What resolution does 3840 × 2160 describe?
options: Full HD (1080p)
4K Ultra HD
720p HD
Standard definition
why: 3840 × 2160 is 4K UHD, four times the pixel count of 1920 × 1080 Full HD.

q: Why do animators make a quick low-quality preview (a playblast) before the final render?
options: A playblast is used as the final render, so no other render is needed
A playblast adds sound effects to the animation automatically
It checks motion and timing quickly without waiting for full-quality frames
A playblast exports the model and its animation to a game engine
why: A playblast captures the viewport fast, letting animators review timing before spending hours on final rendering.

q: What is a script used for in a 3D program?
options: Writing the dialogue that the characters speak in the film
Painting textures by hand directly onto the model's surface
Recording the actors' voices for the characters' lines
Automating repetitive tasks with code
why: Scripts (for example Python in Maya or Blender) automate repeated steps and build custom tools.

q: A rigger builds one control that curls all five fingers into a fist at once. What is the benefit?
options: Animators can pose a complex part faster and more consistently
The hand renders without textures, which makes the scene lighter
The fingers can no longer be moved one at a time by the animator
The model's file size doubles, which improves the hand's detail
why: Exposing one high-level control for a complex action speeds up animation and keeps poses consistent.

q: In a compositing program, what does an adjustment layer do?
options: It permanently deletes the pixels of the layers below it
It applies effects to the layers below without altering them
It adds a new camera that the composition can be viewed through
It exports the finished composition as the final movie file
why: An adjustment layer carries effects such as color correction that affect the layers beneath it non-destructively.

q: Why do compositors often receive CG renders split into passes such as diffuse, specular, and shadow?
options: Splitting the render into passes turns the image black and white
Rendering in passes removes the need to light the 3D scene
Each pass can be adjusted separately without re-rendering
Separate passes are required so the sound can be mixed later
why: Separate passes let the compositor tweak reflections, shadows, or color individually, saving costly re-renders.

q: What is a fade to black often used to signal?
options: That the camera malfunctioned during filming
An instant jump to the very next moment
That a sound effect is about to play
The end of a scene or a major break in time
why: Fading to black closes a scene or chapter and gives the audience a pause before what comes next.

q: Why might a compositor feather the edge of a mask?
options: To soften the edge so the cut-out blends naturally
To make the mask invisible to everyone viewing the composition
To add a sound effect at the moment the masked area appears
To increase the frame rate of the footage inside the mask
why: Feathering blurs the mask boundary so the masked area transitions smoothly instead of showing a hard, cut-out edge.

q: Why should a green screen be lit evenly?
options: Even light makes the actors' skin and clothing look greener on camera
Even color lets the keyer remove the background more cleanly
Even light removes the need to use a keyer during compositing
Even light makes the footage black and white for easier editing
why: Shadows and hot spots create several shades of green, which are harder to key out without damaging the subject.

q: A handheld shot is too shaky. Which tracking-based tool can smooth it out?
options: Keylight
A spill suppressor
Stabilization (such as Warp Stabilizer)
A cross-dissolve
why: Stabilizers track the motion in the shot and counter-move the frame to remove unwanted shake.

q: Why should the edit's frame rate match the frame rate of the rendered frames?
options: Matching the frame rate makes the exported file much smaller
The frame rate setting controls the colors of the final image
Matching frame rates removes the need for any sound in the edit
Mismatched rates make motion stutter and drift out of sync with sound
why: If 24 fps frames are placed in a 30 fps timeline without care, motion stutters or changes speed and audio no longer lines up.

q: Which audio format is uncompressed and commonly used for high-quality sound in post-production?
options: MP3
AAC
WAV
OGG
why: WAV stores uncompressed audio, so it keeps full quality for editing and mixing; MP3, AAC, and OGG are lossy delivery formats.
